n4-arau.meaning_mnemonic: Someone plants their <radical>human legs</radical> wide in the shallows, bracing against the current. Three <radical>water</radical> droplets flick off a passing paintbrush into their face, then the whole current joins in, sluicing down their legs until every stain gets scrubbed clean. Wash.
n4-arau.reading_mnemonic: Downstream at the same riverbank, a heron named <reading>Sen</reading> watches the whole scrubbing with total calm, muttering one flat <reading>せん</reading> every time a sock goes under. She's heard it all before, standing on one leg exactly where the current runs coldest.

n4-ba.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, someone hammers a signpost into the <radical>earth</radical>, staking out one square patch of level <radical>ground</radical>, and every <radical>day</radical> the sun climbs up right over that same stake, marking the exact spot all over again. Sun after sun, the marker never moves — that patch has become a place.
n4-ba.reading_mnemonic: A fisherman named <reading>Joe</reading> claims that same staked patch every single morning, plants his stool right on the marker, and grunts <reading>じょう</reading> at anyone who dares set foot on his place at the riverbank.

n4-chi.meaning_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, the wooden signpost planted in the <radical>earth</radical> isn't alone — beside its base, the last coiled loop of a snake's tail sits frozen in that same dirt, simply continuing <radical>to be</radical>. Sign and tail, both staked into the same patch of soil: together they mark out this exact stretch as ground.
n4-chi.reading_mnemonic: Still on that trail, a hiker named <reading>Cheech</reading> stubs his toe on the signpost and yelps <reading>ち</reading> — cheese! — hopping backward straight into the motionless snake tail, which doesn't so much as flinch.

n4-dou.meaning_mnemonic: A wide box drops onto the level <radical>ground</radical> right outside Koichi's konbini, three walls up and no floor, blocking the door. You crouch down to peer through its open front — that's exactly the <radical>wide box</radical> you know — and staring back out of the gloom is a <radical>mouth</radical>, yawning out the very order you were about to say yourself, word for word. Same ground, same box, same mouth: same.
n4-dou.reading_mnemonic: Back at Koichi's konbini, the mouth belongs to the onigiri baker, elbow-deep in <reading>dough</reading> behind the counter. Every time you ask what's going on, he just grunts <reading>どう</reading> without looking up — same shrug, same word, same batch of dough, every single time you ask.

n4-gyou.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>sheep</radical> plants its four stiff legs on the level <radical>ground</radical> beneath a <radical>tree</radical>, hangs a little sign off a low branch, and spends the whole day there chewing calmly through paperwork, unbothered and punctual, running its own steady little trade. This is the sheep's business.
n4-gyou.reading_mnemonic: Every morning a regular customer named <reading>Geo</reading> strolls up to the sheep's stand under the tree, and the sheep bleats <reading>ぎょう</reading> back at him like a receipt stamping shut — same tree, same ground, same bleat, business as usual.

n4-hajimeru.meaning_mnemonic: In the school locker room a silkworm has just sealed itself into its <radical>cocoon</radical>, when the star dancer bursts in yawning her <radical>mouth</radical> wide open, and mid-yawn her legs snap into that crossed, arms-flung stance of a <radical>woman</radical> about to perform. The cocoon splits open in that instant — this is where everything begins.
n4-hajimeru.reading_mnemonic: The coach doesn't shout 'go' — she just says <reading>し</reading>, flat and clipped like the English word <reading>she</reading>, and that single syllable is the starting gun for the dancer, the silkworm, and everyone else still stretching by the lockers.

n4-hashiru.meaning_mnemonic: The signpost that's usually planted still in the <radical>earth</radical>, crossbar and flat soil baseline undisturbed for years, suddenly rips itself loose and bolts down the mountain trail, dragging a ragged tail of dirt behind it, going faster than a plain wooden post has any business going. Somehow, it is now running.
n4-hashiru.reading_mnemonic: Hikers at the top of the trail gasp <reading>そう</reading> — a drawn-out sound just like the English word <reading>sew</reading> — as the loose signpost sprints past the vending machine, and one startled hiker keeps repeating it long after the post is gone.

n4-hataraku.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>person</radical> hauls up the mountain trail before dawn, one <radical>power</radical>-flexed arm dragging them past the vending machine, while the <radical>sun</radical> crawls across the sky, until both boots hit solid <radical>ground</radical> at the summit — soaked, aching, still not done. That sunrise-to-sunset climb is work.
n4-hataraku.reading_mnemonic: At the very top, a badger named <reading>Dobu</reading> slumps against that same vending machine and groans <reading>どう</reading> into the empty air — not a question, just the sound of a body that has decided the climb was too much work.

n4-hatsu.meaning_mnemonic: Off the blocks, the <radical>outspread legs</radical> explode sideways and collapse into a wincing split. The racer's <radical>human legs</radical> land planted wide just as <radical>two</radical> chopsticks clatter off a dropped bento — chasing a train already hissing steam, pulling away without them.
n4-hatsu.reading_mnemonic: On the platform, a conductor named <reading>Hatsu</reading> slams the doors and yells <reading>はつ</reading> into his whistle as steam bursts from the wheels — one word, and the train is already gone.

n4-hiku.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, past the improbable vending machine, an archer plants their feet and hauls back on a springy <radical>bow</radical>, bending its stacked-curve wood taut until the string bites into their fingers. That single act of hauling back is the whole meaning: to pull.
n4-hiku.reading_mnemonic: A parrot named Inko perches on the vending machine and screeches <reading>いん</reading> the instant the string snaps taut, like an <reading>inn</reading> bell ringing for a guest who arrived too fast. Every hiker on the trail flinches at the sound before they even see the arrow.

n4-hou.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 方 as one warped signpost bolted into a crossroads. Its crossbar arm won't hold still — it spins in the wind until it locks facing one direction, and a lost traveler grabs the swinging arm just to have something to follow. One pole, one direction, and the person now walking it.
n4-hou.reading_mnemonic: An owl called <reading>Hoot</reading> lands on the swinging signpost's crossbar and states the obvious in one flat call, <reading>ほう</reading>, every single time the arm swings past true north.
n4-hou.description: 万 is simpler than it looks: one long horizontal capped by a single sweeping curve that swings down and left into a hook, nothing above it. 方 carries an extra short tick above its crossbar before the vertical stroke kicks left and hooks at the bottom — that top tick is the tell. No tick, it's 万; tick present, it's 方.

n4-ie-kanji.meaning_mnemonic: The pigeon sliding belly-first down that slick <radical>roof</radical> shoots off the eaves and through an open window, landing on the <radical>pig</radical> mid belly-rub, legs already kicking the air in outrage. Pig and pigeon end up tangled on one floor under one roof — and a roof with a pig living underneath, indignities and all, is what makes a house a house.
n4-ie-kanji.reading_mnemonic: Kaa the fire-breathing crow perches on the power line outside that house, unimpressed by the racket inside. Every time the pig squeals and kicks at the ceiling, she tips her head back and lets out one flat <reading>か</reading> — a dry little <reading>kah</reading> of judgment, then goes back to smoking her own beak.

n4-isogu.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>broom</radical>'s cat sleeps through it, so crumbs and cat skid down the hallway too fast to stop. Someone chasing it yanks the <radical>wrap</radical> tighter around the watermelon, and the jolt sets the <radical>heart</radical> — hook flicking, three drops flung loose — pounding in a full panicked sprint. Everyone hurries.
n4-isogu.reading_mnemonic: Skidding into that same hallway, a courier pigeon named <reading>Cue</reading> can't stop in time and slams into the pile, wheezing out a strangled <reading>きゅう</reading> as crumbs and feathers go flying. He's always this late, and it's always this loud.

n4-ji-self.meaning_mnemonic: The staring <radical>eye</radical> that watches everything finally gets curious about itself. It swivels all the way around until it's pressed right up against a cracked mirror in Sei's school bathroom, pupil to pupil with its own reflection — recognizing, for the very first time, itself.
n4-ji-self.reading_mnemonic: Still at that mirror, a boy named <reading>Jeeves</reading> catches his own stare looking back and mutters <reading>じ</reading> — jeez — mortified that of everyone in the school, he's the one caught staring at himself.
n4-ji-self.description: 自 opens with a short diagonal tick above the top-left corner of the box — a stroke that 目 simply doesn't have; 目 is a plain, evenly-ruled rectangle with two level bars inside. 白 carries that same top tick, but its box is shorter and squarer with only a single centered bar, reading flatter and more compact than 自's taller, narrower frame.

n4-kai.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>cocoon</radical> sealed in the locker room splits open, and a <radical>person</radical> steps out mid-stride, heading for the corner table. There, <radical>two</radical> chopsticks sit crossed and waiting, set for one more guest — the cocoon opened right on time, because someone was coming to meet them.
n4-kai.reading_mnemonic: At that corner table, a boy named <reading>Kai</reading> waves both arms so hard the chopsticks clatter, shouting <reading>かい</reading> down the hallway so his cocoon-fresh friend won't miss the table.
n4-kai.description: 会 and 今 share the same person-shaped lid on top, but diverge below it: 会 stacks two flat strokes above a closed loop that seals shut at the bottom, giving it a boxed look. 今 has one flat stroke and a hook that swoops open to the lower right — no closed loop anywhere in it.

n4-kariru.meaning_mnemonic: Every <radical>day</radical>, as the sun climbs behind that little windowpane, a <radical>person</radical> strides in from the left and swipes <radical>two</radical> chopsticks off next door's table — promising to bring them back before the window goes dark again. It isn't stealing if you plan to return it; it's borrowing.
n4-kariru.reading_mnemonic: The neighbor doesn't even look up. She just hears a stray cat named <reading>Shaku</reading> hiss <reading>しゃく</reading> from the doorway — her signal that her chopsticks have gone wandering again and will be back by dinner.
n4-kariru.description: 借りる marks the side receiving something on loan — you end up holding an item that isn't yours yet. The opposite motion, handing something over to someone else, is a completely different kanji; don't let the shared idea of a loan blur which direction this one points.

n4-kasu.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>person</radical> strides in from the left, hammers a <radical>stake</radical> into the square, banner flapping, then tips open the clam-shell wallet — coins spilling from the <radical>money</radical> shell into open hands. The flag stays planted as a record of what was handed over, and to whom: this is lending.
n4-kasu.reading_mnemonic: By the planted stake, a goat named <reading>Tai</reading> headbutts the empty shell and bleats <reading>たい</reading>, annoyed that all the coins are already gone — lent out before she got her share.
n4-kasu.description: 貸す marks the side handing something over — you're the one giving up temporary use of something. The receiving side of that same transaction is a completely different kanji; keep the direction straight instead of leaning on the shared idea of a loan.

n4-ken-exam.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>horse</radical> gallops in, all boxy body and dust-kicking hooves, expecting a race. Instead a vet in a lab coat pins it to a scale, shines a light in its eyes, and checks its teeth one by one. The horse stamps and snorts, furious, but every inch of it gets examined before it's ever let out to run.
n4-ken-exam.reading_mnemonic: Ken, the sword-collecting dog, guards the clinic door with a wall of antique blades gleaming behind him. Every time the horse tries to bolt past without finishing its checkup, Ken barks one sharp <reading>けん</reading> — <reading>Ken</reading> means nobody skips the exam.

n4-koto.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>broom</radical> keeps shoving the indignant cat down the hallway, crumbs and cat alike skidding across the level <radical>ground</radical>, until the whole heap finally piles up in front of a <radical>mouth</radical> — which snaps wide open, mid-yawn, and reports the entire incident as one official matter, filed and done.
n4-koto.reading_mnemonic: In Sei's school hallway, a kid who watched the whole cat-and-broom pileup yelps <reading>jeez</reading>, then gets marched off to file it with the teacher as an official <reading>じ</reading> — a matter now on the record, whether he wanted it there or not.

n4-kyou-teach.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>old</radical> teacher shuffles to the desk, unhurried, cane dragging. A <radical>child</radical> bursts in, arms flung wide, bundled and eager. The elder rears that cane back over one shoulder and cracks it down in one furious <radical>tap</radical> — the child freezes, listening. That crack is how you teach.
n4-kyou-teach.reading_mnemonic: Kyo, the new teaching assistant, flinches every time the cane cracks against the desk and yelps <reading>きょう</reading> before she can stop herself. By the third lesson the whole class waits for her <reading>Kyo</reading>-shaped shriek before they even hear the tap.

n4-mise.meaning_mnemonic: Nailed into the cliff with nothing underneath, that lean-to <radical>shelter</radical> gets a tenant: a tortoise who reads cracks in its own shell for <radical>divination</radical>, shouting today's fortune to anyone passing. A wide <radical>mouth</radical> yawns open below as the doorway, swallowing customers whole to hear it. Shelter, fortune-teller, doorway — it's officially a shop.
n4-mise.reading_mnemonic: A customer ducks through the yawning mouth-shaped doorway, drops exactly <reading>ten</reading> coins on the tortoise's card table, and gets his fortune shouted back in one flat syllable, <reading>てん</reading>, then returns every week for the same price.

n4-mono.meaning_mnemonic: Every day, the same stooped shuffle you know as <radical>old</radical> reappears at the crosswalk just as the sun climbs behind that little barred window marking a new <radical>day</radical>, and traffic idles while it crosses. Rain or shine, that shuffle is the one figure the neighborhood recognizes — not by name, just as a person who shows up every day.
n4-mono.reading_mnemonic: The driver stuck idling at that crosswalk, a man named <reading>Shuji</reading>, finally leans on his horn and shouts <reading>しゃ</reading> — shoo! — at the shuffling old figure, who doesn't even glance up before finishing the crossing at exactly the same pace.
n4-mono.description: 者 almost never stands alone as a word; it works as a suffix stitched onto a verb or field to name whoever does it, much the way English -er turns 'teach' into 'teacher'. Learning it as a floating idea of a person is the right starting point, but expect to meet it glued onto the end of something else far more often than by itself.

n4-motsu.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>hand</radical> reaches in from the kanji's left edge and closes around the carpenter's ruler notched for a single <radical>inch</radical>, then rams its end down into the <radical>earth</radical> like the mossy shrine signpost, refusing to let go until the plot is measured. That white-knuckle grip is what it means: to hold.
n4-motsu.reading_mnemonic: The groundskeeper who plants that ruler in the dirt every morning is named <reading>Jee</reading> — one flat syllable, <reading>じ</reading> — and he grunts it out loud each time he drives the measure into the ground, like a stamp confirming the hold is solid.

n4-omou.meaning_mnemonic: You stand at the edge of your flooded <radical>rice field</radical>, its paths crossing the plots into a grid below you. Above it your wounded <radical>heart</radical> drags itself up and hovers there, thumping, while you stare at the grid, turning the harvest over one square at a time. That thumping stillness is what it looks like to think.
n4-omou.reading_mnemonic: A heron named Shi stands dead still over the rice field, chewing over something enormous. Every few minutes it snaps its beak and lets out one flat <reading>し</reading> — proof that all that stillness is <reading>Shi</reading>'s thought, not sleep.

n4-owaru.meaning_mnemonic: Grandma Kane sits on the shrine steps unspooling a length of <radical>thread</radical>, fibers fraying at the tip, and tied to the very end is a duckling towed along by its <radical>trailing foot</radical>, webbed foot skidding on the mossy stone. The spool runs out, the duckling skids to a stop at her feet, and there is nowhere left to go — that's the end.
n4-owaru.reading_mnemonic: The instant the thread runs out, one of the shrine cats pounces and clamps its teeth on what's left of the duckling's lace like it's stealing a <reading>shoe</reading> — its triumphant yowl comes out as <reading>しゅう</reading>, the exact sound of the last stretch of thread giving way.

n4-sha.meaning_mnemonic: On orientation day, the new hires drive the <radical>earth</radical> signpost into the ground behind Grandma Kane's shrine, right beside the stone <radical>altar</radical> where offerings sit out for everyone to see. Stake in the soil, altar in front of it — that's a company: a group planted on its own ground, showing itself off to the world.
n4-sha.reading_mnemonic: Still behind the shrine, a new hire named <reading>Shae</reading> trips over the freshly staked signpost and yelps <reading>しゃ</reading> as she stumbles face-first into the altar's offering tray — her first day at the company already the stuff of legend.
n4-sha.description: 社 originally named the local earth god's shrine — the altar raised on a patch of claimed ground for a village's protector spirit. The word later stretched to cover any group organized around a shared institution, which is why it equally means a shrine and a company: the modern sense kept the idea of a formal body bound to a place, not the religious content.

n4-shi-try.meaning_mnemonic: At the ceremony marking a new <radical>construction</radical> site, someone hammers the flagged <radical>stake</radical> into the dirt to mark exactly where the girder will go, then clears their throat and gives it a go — a shaky <radical>speech</radical>, words bubbling out of the mouth one line at a time, nobody rehearsed, just to see if it works. Stake planted, girder not even up yet, speech barely holding together: that shaky first attempt is the very definition of a try.
n4-shi-try.reading_mnemonic: A foreman named <reading>Shii</reading> paces around the ceremony, hissing a stressed <reading>し</reading> through his teeth every time the speech wobbles, certain the whole shaky test is about to collapse before the stake even settles into the ground.

n4-shin-heart.meaning_mnemonic: That dragging fishhook flicks upward one final time, flinging its three blood drops clear across the tackle box, and beneath the hook you can still feel it, thudding out of rhythm every time the line goes taut. The whole hook has become nothing but one wounded, thumping <radical>heart</radical>, still working even torn open.
n4-shin-heart.reading_mnemonic: A dockside medic named <reading>Shin</reading> presses a stethoscope to the hook and hears it clearly, <reading>しん</reading>, <reading>しん</reading>, ragged but steady, the same wounded rhythm from the tackle box.
n4-shin-heart.description: 必, the kanji for necessary, is this same wounded heart with one extra diagonal stroke slashed clean through it from upper right to lower left, like a blade cutting across where 心 has nothing but hook and blood. A line piercing straight through the middle marks 必; the bare hook and three loose drops with nothing crossing them is 心.

n4-shinu.meaning_mnemonic: The raccoon is still airborne, gripping the bent <radical>spoon</radical> from that badly leveraged scoop of ice cream, and comes down hard on the already-cracked corner of <radical>death / bad luck</radical>. The bone gives way completely under the impact, nothing left to set or straighten. That's the whole story: die.
n4-shinu.reading_mnemonic: Behind the register at Koichi's konbini, the cashier named <reading>She</reading> hears the crash and doesn't even look up, just breathes one flat <reading>し</reading> and rings up the shattered tub anyway. Nothing about tonight is going to surprise her.

n4-shiru.meaning_mnemonic: On Sei's sports field, an <radical>arrow</radical> streaks straight across the grass and thunks dead center into the target, and in that same instant your <radical>mouth</radical> snaps open with the answer — no hesitation, just the fact flying out as fast and true as the shot. That instant, certain hit is knowing something.
n4-shiru.reading_mnemonic: Chibi the parrot roosts on that same target and shrieks <reading>ち</reading> the second the arrow lands, confirming the answer before you can even say it out loud — a sharp <reading>chee</reading> of certainty every time.

n4-shitsu.meaning_mnemonic: A dart drifts across the room, finally tips into its slow dive, and thuds point-first into the floorboards, quivering upright exactly where it has come to <radical>arrive</radical>. It lands directly under the sagging edge of a slick <radical>roof</radical>, and the patch of floor boxed in by that overhang — dart standing sentry in the middle of it — becomes a room all its own.
n4-shitsu.reading_mnemonic: A landlady everyone calls <reading>Shitsu</reading> stomps in to inspect the new room, presses her ear to the dart still quivering in the floorboards, and grunts a flat <reading>しつ</reading> of approval before stamping the doorframe and moving to the next one.

n4-tobu.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the whole character at once: two wings snapped open mid-beat, feathers combing the air on both sides, and a tail feather trailing straight back like it's still catching up. Nothing about the shape sits still — every stroke leans into the same direction, caught at the exact instant the ground lets go. That's fly.
n4-tobu.reading_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, past the lone vending machine, a paper crane named <reading>Hee</reading> catches an updraft and lifts clean off the ground. She lets out one thin <reading>ひ</reading> of surprise and doesn't come back down before the trail bends out of sight.

n4-tokoro.meaning_mnemonic: Right outside the door that never latches, the raccoon-dented one still swinging on its hinge, stands a stump with the woodsman's <radical>axe</radical> still buried in it — nobody ever pulled it back out. Meet me by the axe that never came out, right by the <radical>door</radical> that won't shut: that spot is the place everyone in town can point to.
n4-tokoro.reading_mnemonic: A mailman circles the stump twice before he's sure, then stamps the address form with one flat syllable, <reading>しょ</reading>, like he's about to <reading>show</reading> you exactly where to stand, axe and swinging door included.

n4-tsukau.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, a <radical>person</radical> plants both feet on one patch of <radical>ground</radical> and flings their <radical>mouth</radical> wide, bellowing orders at everyone scrubbing laundry in the shallows — never lifting a hand, just pointing. That bossy, hands-off stance is use: someone else's effort put to work on your command.
n4-tsukau.reading_mnemonic: Shiba the heron struts along that same riverbank, screeching orders of his own at the laundry crew like a tiny drill sergeant — the sound comes out as a piercing <reading>し</reading>, pure <reading>sheesh</reading>, every single time someone slacks off scrubbing.

n4-uta.meaning_mnemonic: You drag up Grandma Kane's mossy shrine steps, one <radical>ground</radical>-level stair at a time, powered by nothing but a <radical>lack</radical> of energy — the kind that ends in a yawn. At the top your <radical>mouth</radical> cracks wide open, and instead of a yawn, a full song pours out, echoing off the bell until every cat bolts.
n4-uta.reading_mnemonic: Kaa the fire-breathing crow lands on that same shrine bell mid-echo and answers your song with his own — not a caw but a scorched-throat <reading>か</reading>, <reading>Kaa</reading>, puffing a little ring of fire that singes the moss every time he hits the note.

n4-zu.meaning_mnemonic: Trapped inside a solid <radical>enclosure</radical> — four unbroken walls, no door, no window, no way out no matter which way you circle — someone stops walking and starts scratching lines into the plaster instead, every corner already paced, every dead turn, inked onto the inside of the wall. That scribbled record of the walk is now a diagram, a map of nothing but itself.
n4-zu.reading_mnemonic: A surveyor everyone calls <reading>Zuzu</reading> gets called in to examine the scratched walls, traces one finger along the lines, and grunts a single <reading>ず</reading> of approval — first map she's ever seen that doubles as a cry for help.
